items.title: MemoryDojo: Benchmarking Poisoning Through LLM Agent Memory
items.summary_1line: LLM agents benefit from using memory systems to improve performance on long-horizon, multi-session tasks. However, memory introduces a critical attack surface. Malicious instructions encountered in one session may be...
items.editor_note: Shifts the focus to security: memory persisting across sessions as a poisoning path.

editorial.tldr: In October a paper benchmarked personal agent memory on interaction preferences, asking whether agents stop re-asking what users already told them. In early November, two more benchmarks moved the question from convenience to correctness and security.
editorial.whats_new: MemoryDojo (Nov 6) is a benchmark for poisoning attacks through LLM agent memory, where malicious instructions seen in one session can carry into later ones.
editorial.why_it_matters: Agent memory is now being evaluated for three distinct failure modes (burdensome re-asking, hallucinated memory, poisoning), so a memory layer needs tests for each, not just recall.
editorial.take_for_builders: If your agent persists memory across sessions, add a test that plants an instruction in one session and checks it is not acted on in the next, and treat stored memory as untrusted input.

status.detail: Three arXiv benchmarks in about two weeks each probe a different way agent memory can fail.
